overview: The Returning SBA to Main Street Act would require the Small Business Administration (SBA), the federal agency that helps small businesses with loans and counseling, to move at least 30 percent of its headquarters employees to SBA offices outside the Washington, D.C., area within a year, but only if the SBA head finds the move would lower costs for the government. Moved workers would be paid at the local pay rate for their new location and could not telework full time, and other full-time teleworkers who stay in the D.C. area would lose full-time telework as well, with an exception for employees who telework as a disability accommodation. The bill also requires the SBA to cut its headquarters office space by at least 30 percent within two years and to report staffing and telework numbers to Congress each year. It states that it overrides conflicting laws and union contracts and that employees cannot sue to challenge decisions made under it. As of March 4, 2025, the Senate Small Business Committee had approved it with changes and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say moving staff out of Washington puts SBA employees closer to the small businesses they serve, especially in rural areas, while reducing costly headquarters space, and the cost-savings condition guards against moves that would waste money.
against: Critics say forced relocations and the end of full-time telework could push experienced staff to quit and disrupt service, and that overriding union agreements and barring lawsuits leaves affected workers little recourse.
